The Blessed One said this: “Bhikkhus, just as whatever there is of footprints in the world, the elephant’s footprint is declared their chief by way of size; so too, among all wholesome qualities, the noble eightfold path is declared their chief. And what, bhikkhus, is that noble eightfold path? It is right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration. This, bhikkhus, is that noble eightfold path. “Just as, bhikkhus, whatever there is of footprints in the world, the elephant’s footprint is declared their chief by way of size, so too, among all wholesome qualities, the noble eightfold path is declared their chief. “Just as, bhikkhus, the great ocean has a single taste, the taste of salt, so too, this Dhamma and Discipline have a single taste, the taste of liberation. “Just as, bhikkhus, the river Ganges slants, slopes, and inclines towards the east, so too, this community of bhikkhus slants, slopes, and inclines towards nibbāna. “Just as, bhikkhus, a cowherd boy with a staff in his hand tends a herd of cattle to the pasture ground, so too, the Tathāgata, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, tends the community of bhikkhus with the staff of the Dhamma. “Just as, bhikkhus, a skilled butcher or butcher’s apprentice, having slaughtered a cow, might carve it up with a sharp carving knife, so too, the Tathāgata, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, having cut off the conceit ‘I am’ with its underlying tendency, has carved up the mass of suffering. “Just as, bhikkhus, a skilled goldsmith or goldsmith’s apprentice, having placed gold in a furnace, might blow upon it with a bellows, so too, the Tathāgata, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, having placed the mind in the furnace of wisdom, might blow upon it with the bellows of concentration. “Just as, bhikkhus, a skilled ivory-worker or ivory-worker’s apprentice, having taken an elephant tusk, might carve it up with a sharp carving knife, so too, the Tathāgata, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, having cut off the conceit ‘I am’ with its underlying tendency, has carved up the mass of suffering. “Just as, bhikkhus, a skilled carpenter or carpenter’s apprentice, having taken a piece of wood, might carve it up with a sharp adze, so too, the Tathāgata, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, having cut off the conceit ‘I am’ with its underlying tendency, has carved up the mass of suffering. “Just as, bhikkhus, when a skilled elephant trainer has trained an elephant, he would mount him and ride him out for exercise; so too, when the Tathāgata, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One has trained the mind, he would mount it and ride it out for exercise. “Just as, bhikkhus, when a skilled horse trainer has trained a horse, he would mount him and ride him out for exercise; so too, when the Tathāgata, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One has trained the mind, he would mount it and ride it out 20. ||| The twenty-first chapter of the *Aṣṭasāhasrikā Prajñāpāramitā* is concluded. ||| Chapter Twenty-One: The Chapter on the Non-Existence of All Dharmas. ||| Subhūti addressed the Blessed One: "Blessed One, it is wonderful how this *prajñāpāramitā* is the mother of the Bodhisattvas, the great beings. The Blessed One said: "Subhūti, it is so; it is as you say. This *prajñāpāramitā* is indeed the mother of the Bodhisattvas, the great beings. Subhūti asked: "Blessed One, why is this *prajñāpāramitā* the mother of the Bodhisattvas, the great beings? The Blessed One replied: "Subhūti, because by means of this *prajñāpāramitā*, the Bodhisattvas, the great beings, fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment. Furthermore, Subhūti, this *prajñāpāramitā* is the progenitor of the Bodhisattvas, the great beings. Why is that? Because, Subhūti, all dharmas are unproduced (*anutpanna*). Subhūti, what do you think? Is there any dharma whatsoever that has been produced? Subhūti said: "No, Blessed One. The Blessed One said: "Subhūti, it is for this reason that this *prajñāpāramitā* is the progenitor of the Bodhisattvas, the great beings. Subhūti asked: "Blessed One, if all dharmas are unproduced, then what is the dharma that the Bodhisattva, the great being, should fully awaken to as unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment? The Blessed One said: "Subhūti, even that very dharma which is called 'unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment'—that dharma does not exist, nor is it to be found. Subhūti asked: "Blessed One, if that dharma does not exist and is not to be found, then how can a Bodhisattva, a great being, fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment? The Blessed One said: "Subhūti, it is precisely because that dharma does not exist and is not to be found that a Bodhisattva, a great being, fully awakens to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment. Why is that? Subhūti, if that dharma were existent and could be found, then a Bodhisattva, a great being, would not fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment. It is because that dharma is non-existent and cannot be found that a Bodhisattva, a great being, fully awakens to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment. Furthermore, Subhūti, that which is called 'the realm of phenomena' (*dharmadhātu*), that is not a realm, and thus it is called 'the realm of phenomena. That which is called 'the realm of space' (*ākāśadhātu*), that is not a realm, and thus it is called 'the realm of space. Subhūti, it is in this way that a Bodhisattva, a great being, should train in this *prajñāpāramitā*. 1. “The Blessed One has said: ‘Monks, there are these four kinds of persons found existing in the world. What four? They are: the person who goes from darkness to darkness; the person who goes from darkness to light; the person who goes from light to darkness; and the person who goes from light to light. And what, monks, is the person who goes from darkness to darkness? Here, monks, someone is reborn in a low family—a family of outcasts, bamboo-workers, hunters, basket-makers, or flower-removers—a poor family with little food and drink, where life is difficult and sustenance is hard to find. There he is ugly, unsightly, and ill-favored, with limbs that are deformed, eyes that are clouded, and a face that is blotchy. He is also dull-witted, slow in understanding, and lacks wisdom. He does not gain wealth through his own effort, nor does he gain great fame. He does not obtain a high position, nor does he obtain a wife, nor does he obtain children, nor does he obtain livestock, nor does he obtain grain. He is also afflicted by many diseases: he suffers from chronic headaches, or from fever, or from chills, or from dysentery, or from abdominal dropsy, or from hemorrhoids, or from fistula, or from consumption, or from epilepsy. He is also short-lived, often struck by calamities, and dies young. Having passed away from here, he is reborn in a state of misery, a bad destination, the lower world, or in hell. This, monks, is called the person who goes from darkness to darkness. And what, monks, is the person who goes from darkness to light? Here, monks, someone is reborn in a low family—a family of outcasts, bamboo-workers, hunters, basket-makers, or flower-removers—a poor family with little food and drink, where life is difficult and sustenance is hard to find. The *pravara* for the Gārgyāyaṇa gotra is Bhārgava, Cyavana, Āpnavāna, Aurva, and Jamadagni. The *pravara* for the Garga gotra is Kāśyapa, Avatsāra, and Śāṇḍila. The *pravara* for the Śātādvāravāsinī gotra is Gārmya, Gārgi, and Śaṅkha. The *pravara* for the Śeṣarudha gotra is Āṅgirasa, Āmbarīṣa, and Yauvanāśva.

The Vatsa lineage has the *gotra* of Gocaja and the *pravara* of Jñānajā: Bhārgava, Cyāvana, Āpraghāna, and Aurva-Purodhasa. The Vātsya lineage has the *gotra* of Gocaja and the *pravara* of Jñānajā: Bhārgava, Cyāvana, Āpraghāna, and Aurva-Purodhasa. The Vātsya lineage has the *gotra* of Gocaja and the *pravara* of Śīharī: Bhārgava, Cyāvana, and Āpyuvān, [with] Aurva-Purodhasa. The Śyāpāyana lineage has the *gotra* of Gocaja and the *pravara* of Śīdarī: Bhārgava, Cyāvana, and Āpyuvān, [with] Aurva-Purodhasa. Śyāma, Jamadagni, and Dhāraṇa constitute the *gotra* of the Dhāraṇa lineage; its *gotra*-born [descendants] have the *pravara* of Chrajā.
